svg.font-family: Segoe UI, Helvetica Neue, Arial, sans-serif
svg.text: What actually happens at the handout desk
Five steps, about four seconds, and nobody types anything.
The employee scans their card
A handheld or desk scanner reads the badge and types the employee's email into the
app's text box, then sends an Enter — exactly as a keyboard would. Nobody touches a
mouse and nobody spells a surname out loud across a queue.
The box is focused the moment the screen opens and re-arms itself after every scan, so a
queue of forty people is forty scans and nothing else.
txtScan.Text → "dev@jgalili.onmicrosoft.com"
Their uncollected rows are found
The email from the badge is matched against the list's person column, and any batch
already marked as printed is dropped. What is left is what they have not yet been
given, however many codes each of those rows happens to be carrying.
Already collected everything? The screen says so by name and count, so the desk can
explain rather than guess. An unrecognised badge gets its own, different message.
Filter(colAll, Printed <> true)
One row becomes many cards
The codes live crammed into a single text cell, separated by semicolons. They get split
apart so that each one becomes its own record, carrying the batch name and the
employee's name along with it.
Two rows holding five codes become five cards. Blank entries — the kind a stray trailing
semicolon leaves behind — are dropped, so nobody is handed an empty voucher.
Ungroup(AddColumns(…, Split(QRCodes, ";")), "Codes")
The desk sees them before printing
Every voucher appears on screen as a card: batch name, barcode, the code in plain
text, and whose it is. The person at the desk can see at a glance that the right name is
on the right vouchers before a single sheet of paper is used.
The code is always printed as text beside its barcode. If anything at all goes wrong with
the bars, the voucher is still redeemable — it just has to be typed instead of scanned.
Gallery over colCards · one card per record
A cloud flow renders the sheet
The cards go to a flow that lays them out as an A4 page and converts it with SharePoint's
own file converter. The barcodes are plain HTML elements, so nothing has to be fetched.
Only once the file exists are the batches marked as collected.
Two cards across, with a rule that forbids splitting one across a page break, so the sheet
cuts cleanly with scissors instead of losing half a barcode.
Convert file → PDF → Patch(Printed: true)
